author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to systemic versus pulmonary perfusion pressure.
Describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.description: An intact heart and a cutaway heart are displayed side by side. Students orient themselves to the gross anatomy and learn why left/right are described from the patient's perspective.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Orient to the anatomical position of the heart (apex down and to the left).
Understand that left and right are described from the patient's own orientation, reversing the viewer's perspective.
Distinguish the intact exterior view from the cutaway interior view.
instructions: Grab and rotate the two heart models together to view them from any angle.
Note which side is the patient's right and which is the patient's left.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the lab and presents the single intact heart centered for an opening orientation view.
clips.narration: Welcome to the heart anatomy lab. In front of you is a full-size human heart, oriented anatomically with its pointed apex aimed down and slightly to the left, just as it sits in your chest.

clips.changeMeaning: Brings in the cutaway heart beside the intact heart so both exterior and interior views are visible together.
clips.narration: We will study two copies. On the left, the intact heart shows the exterior surface and the great vessels. On the right, a cutaway with the anterior wall removed reveals the four chambers, the septum, and the valves.

clips.changeMeaning: Rotates both hearts slowly to demonstrate the patient-oriented left/right convention and invites student interaction.
clips.narration: An important convention: left and right are named from the patient's perspective, not yours. So the patient's right side appears on your left. Rotate the models to view from any angle.

modules.description: A sequential tour of the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels, with labels appearing on the cutaway view and corresponding regions highlighted on the intact heart.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name the four chambers in anatomical order.
Name the four valves and the structures they separate.
Name the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Map interior structures to exterior landmarks.
instructions: Follow each highlighted structure and read its label.
Note the dual naming of the mitral/bicuspid valve.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the right atrium as the first chamber in the structural tour and shows its label.
clips.narration: We begin our tour with the chambers. The right atrium, in the upper right, receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the highlight and label to the right ventricle, the second chamber.
clips.narration: Below it is the right ventricle, which pumps blood toward the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves highlight to the left atrium and left ventricle to complete the chamber inventory.
clips.narration: On the patient's left, the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs, and the left ventricle, the most muscular chamber, pumps it to the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: Shifts the tour to the four valves, highlighting the tricuspid and pulmonary valves on the right side.
clips.narration: Now the valves. The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle. The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the mitral/bicuspid and aortic valves and notes the dual naming convention for the mitral valve.
clips.narration: On the left, the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve, lies between the left atrium and left ventricle. You will see both names in clinical use. The aortic valve sits between the left ventricle and the aorta.

components.text: Great Vessels: Venae Cavae, Pulmonary Arteries/Veins, Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the major vessels in order and maps them to the intact heart's exterior landmarks.
clips.narration: Finally the great vessels: superior and inferior vena cava bring blood into the right atrium; the pulmonary arteries carry blood to the lungs; the pulmonary veins return it; and the aorta carries blood out to the body. Notice how each interior structure maps to the exterior heart on the left.

modules.description: Color-coded flowing blood fills the cutaway heart, blue for deoxygenated and red for oxygenated, revealing the pulmonary and systemic circuits as two distinct loops.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish deoxygenated (blue) from oxygenated (red) blood by location.
Identify the right side as pumping to the lungs and the left side as pumping to the body.
Differentiate the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit.
instructions: Observe each circuit as it is highlighted in turn.

components.sciptDescription: Animates a continuous flowing-fluid effect along a defined path inside a chamber or vessel. Requires a float 'flowSpeed' set in the inspector and a Transform reference 'pathRoot' marking the start of the flow path. Loops continuously while enabled.

clips.changeMeaning: Fills the right side of the heart with blue flowing deoxygenated blood to establish the color convention.
clips.narration: Blood is color coded here. Blue is deoxygenated. It fills the right side of the heart and the pulmonary arteries heading to the lungs.

components.sciptDescription: Animates a continuous flowing-fluid effect along a defined path inside a chamber or vessel. Requires a float 'flowSpeed' set in the inspector and a Transform reference 'pathRoot' marking the start of the flow path. Loops continuously while enabled.

clips.changeMeaning: Adds the red oxygenated stream on the left side, completing the steady-state two-color pattern.
clips.narration: Red is oxygenated. It fills the left side of the heart, the pulmonary veins returning from the lungs, and the aorta heading out to the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the pulmonary circuit loop by emphasizing the blue-to-lungs path and dimming the systemic stream.
clips.narration: Here is the pulmonary circuit: the right side sends deoxygenated blood to the lungs and receives it back oxygenated. It is a short, low-pressure loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the systemic circuit loop by emphasizing the red-to-body path and dimming the pulmonary stream.
clips.narration: And here is the systemic circuit: the left side sends oxygenated blood to the entire body and receives it back deoxygenated. It is a long, high-pressure loop.

modules.description: A single red blood cell is followed step by step through the complete dual circulation, changing color at the lungs and returning to the start.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace a unit of blood through every chamber, valve, and vessel in correct order.
Identify where the blood changes from deoxygenated to oxygenated.
Reinforce the sequence of the cardiac cycle's contractions.
instructions: Press Next to advance the cell one step along its path.
Replay the trace as many times as you like.

clips.changeMeaning: Places the blue (deoxygenated) blood cell at the superior vena cava as the starting point of the trace.
clips.narration: A single deoxygenated red blood cell, shown blue, enters through the superior vena cava on its way back from the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the cell into the right atrium and through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Pushes the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries toward the lungs.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts, pushing the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries, heading to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: At the lung capillaries the cell visibly changes from blue to red as it picks up oxygen.
clips.narration: In the lung capillaries the cell picks up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. Watch it change from blue to red.

clips.changeMeaning: Returns the now-red cell through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium and through the mitral valve to the left ventricle.
clips.narration: Oxygenated, the cell returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, then passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Pumps the red cell through the aortic valve into the aorta out to the systemic circulation.
clips.narration: The left ventricle contracts powerfully, pushing the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Completes the loop: the cell becomes blue again in the systemic veins and returns to the superior vena cava.
clips.narration: After delivering oxygen to the body's tissues, the cell turns blue again and returns through the systemic veins to the superior vena cava, completing the loop. You may replay the trace anytime.

modules.description: Two cross-sections cut through the ventricles compare the thin right ventricular wall with the much thicker left ventricular wall, with scale markers confirming the roughly 3:1 ratio.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare right and left ventricular myocardial thickness.
Relate wall thickness to the pressure of the systemic versus pulmonary circuit.
Confirm the approximate 3:1 thickness ratio using scale markers.
instructions: Rotate the cross-sections to compare directly.
Read the labeled thickness values and scale markers.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the right ventricle cross-section and labels its thin myocardium.
clips.narration: Here are two cross-sections cut at the same level through the ventricles. The right ventricle, on your left, has a thin wall, only about three to five millimeters.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the left ventricle cross-section and labels its substantially thicker myocardium.
clips.narration: The left ventricle, on your right, has a far thicker wall, roughly ten to fifteen millimeters, about three times thicker.

clips.changeMeaning: Displays a scale marker between the two sections so students can visually confirm the 3:1 thickness ratio and hear the functional explanation.
clips.narration: The reason is functional. The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs, a low-pressure circuit. The left ventricle must drive blood through the entire body against high resistance, so it needs far more muscle. Use the scale marker to confirm the roughly three-to-one ratio.

modules.description: The four valves are categorized as atrioventricular or semilunar and shown in open and closed states across the phases of the cardiac cycle to demonstrate how they prevent backflow.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Categorize valves as atrioventricular (tricuspid, mitral) or semilunar (pulmonary, aortic).
Explain how each valve type prevents backflow.
Identify which valves are open or closed during ventricular contraction and relaxation.
instructions: Step through each valve's open and closed states.
Note which valves are open during contraction versus relaxation.

components.text:
Ventricular Relaxation:
AV Valves OPEN, Semilunar CLOSED

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the atrioventricular valves and shows the AV valve in its open state during ventricular filling.
clips.narration: The atrioventricular valves, the tricuspid and mitral, sit between the atria and ventricles. As the ventricles relax and fill, the AV valves are open, letting blood flow downward.

components.text:
Ventricular Contraction:
AV Valves CLOSED, Semilunar OPEN

clips.changeMeaning: Swaps the AV valve to its closed state and the semilunar valve to open during ventricular contraction.
clips.narration: When the ventricles contract, the AV valves snap shut to stop blood flowing backward into the atria, while the semilunar valves open to let blood out.

clips.changeMeaning: Shows the semilunar valves closing during relaxation to prevent backflow into the ventricles, summarizing valve function.
clips.narration: The semilunar valves, the pulmonary and aortic, then close as the ventricles relax, preventing blood in the arteries from flowing back. Together the valves enforce one-way flow through every beat.

modules.description: The cutaway heart appears unlabeled; the system highlights a structure and the student selects the correct name from candidates, cycling through chambers, valves, and vessels.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall the names of chambers, valves, and vessels without label cues.
Self-assess identification accuracy.
Reinforce the structural inventory through retrieval practice.
instructions: A structure will be highlighted; choose the correct name.
Replay the quiz to reinforce identification.

clips.changeMeaning: Presents the first quiz question by highlighting a chamber and showing three candidate answers.
clips.narration: Identification quiz. Which structure is highlighted here? Select the correct name from the options below.

clips.changeMeaning: Confirms the first answer and advances to a valve identification question with new candidate names.
clips.narration: Correct, that is the right atrium. Next: identify this valve sitting between the right atrium and right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Confirms the valve answer and presents a final vessel identification question.
clips.narration: Correct, the tricuspid valve. Last one: identify this large vessel leaving the left ventricle to carry blood to the body.

modules.description: Given a starting position in the circuit, the student selects the next structure in the path, with emphasis on distinguishing pulmonary arteries from pulmonary veins.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall the sequence of structures in the dual circulation.
Distinguish pulmonary arteries (deoxygenated) from pulmonary veins (oxygenated).
Self-correct misconceptions about flow direction.
instructions: Read the starting position and choose the next structure in the path.
Incorrect answers will remind you of the flow direction.

components.text:
Blood has just entered the Right Atrium.
What is next?

Blood has just entered the Right Atrium.
What is next?

clips.changeMeaning: Presents the first flow-tracing question starting at the right atrium with three valve options.
clips.narration: Flow tracing quiz. Blood has just entered the right atrium. Which structure does it pass through next?

components.text:
Blood leaves the Right Ventricle.
Which vessel carries it to the lungs?

clips.changeMeaning: Advances to the key pulmonary artery versus vein discrimination question after the right ventricle.
clips.narration: Correct, the tricuspid valve. Now blood has been pumped out of the right ventricle. Which vessel carries this deoxygenated blood toward the lungs?

components.text:
Blood is oxygenated in the lungs.
Which vessel returns it to the heart?

clips.changeMeaning: Reinforces the artery/vein distinction and presents the final question about oxygenated return to the left atrium.
clips.narration: Correct. Remember, pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood, the opposite of systemic arteries. Now the blood is oxygenated in the lungs. Which vessel returns it to the left atrium?

modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Review the structural inventory, dual circulation, blood path, wall thickness asymmetry, and valve function.
Consolidate the lab's key takeaways.
instructions: Review each concept area as it is highlighted.

clips.narration: Let's recap. You learned the structural inventory: four chambers, four valves, and the great vessels. You also saw the dual circulation, with the right side serving the lungs and the left side serving the body.

clips.narration: You traced a unit of blood through the entire circuit, and you saw why the left ventricle's wall is about three times thicker than the right's, because it pumps against the high resistance of the whole body.
